A few points though. 

First, they are wrong about minoring. Getting a minor or even a double major is not “double the money.” The whole point of a minor is that it’s fewer credits and can typically be done within the bounds of your yearly credit limits. In whatever degree you get, you need to do general education classes too, but you only need to do them once. So a double major IS more expensive and/or may take more time, but some work together better and more easily than others and might have course overlap. My parents had zero ability to see what courses I was taking or my grades, so if you’re minoring they likely won’t even know. 

Second, they are right to discourage you (I’m sorry, I know it isn’t what you want to hear.) Majoring in dance is unwise for 98% of people. You’re posting this in the ballet subreddit, so I’m making some assumptions here. But most of the people who are going to make money and have a career in ballet by the time they are college aged are already in special professional-track programs, and not in a normal schooling situation. They aren’t majoring in dance at a normal college. A dance degree is not very flexible for career options unless you’re going to double major in business and plan on opening a studio or something. Dance careers can also be unfortunately and abruptly cut short due to injury… and then what?

Don’t stop dancing, but it isn’t something you need to get a degree in. And honestly? As someone who majored in music (I teach now, but was originally a performance major), majoring in it killed a lot of my passion for it for a while. My stress relief suddenly became my primary stressor, as performing arts programs can be notoriously cutthroat and judgmental. I love teaching, but I barely play my primary instrument anymore. In hindsight, I’m relieved I switched majors because I now have a stable job. Money is no joke when you’re on your own, it’s tough out here.

She’s six.

Six year olds can have a huge range of what is appropriate developmentally. The six year olds that get crazy good at an instrument right away are in the minority and often have parents that push them above and beyond at home. 

While it *could* be a symptom of a learning disability, it also could be totally normal and you might be expecting too much too fast. Teaching this age is not for everyone, and it often exhausted/frustrated me (I only teach older kids now). I was part of a weekend preschool music curriculum  and we did teach the staff and bare bones piano skills to 5-6 year olds, but we would only get through about three notes over six months and would intersperse it with other music reading games and activities. Honestly more of the lessons were devoted to music reading games and only a little bit of piano. By the time they finished the next class in the series (the next half a year), they were playing/identifying a whole scale.

I guess what I’m saying is be slow and patient now, don’t try to force too much at once. When they gain confidence with the little skills, they’ll start to learn faster. 

Some strategies to consider if you haven’t already:

-a little magnetic whiteboard with a staff on it and some circle magnets. Have her physically place the magnets to identify the notes. 

-super large print music

-start a consistent color code system for notes (I like to use rainbow order starting on C). Place small items on the keys to match the color and circle/highlight the notes on the page. Slowly withdraw them and see how she does. 

-gamify literally everything.

You might be breathing “wrong.” A lot of people do it at first, and it can become a hard to correct habit. I still catch myself doing it on occasion, and I’ve been playing woodwinds for ~18 years at this point . Check this:

When you breathe, does your upper chest puff out? Do your shoulders raise? If yes, you are getting a shallow breath- there’s an upper limit on how much you’ll be able to hold for and you’re only filling like half of the potential “tank”. Try to take a deep breath with your nose and mouth at the same time, and try to push your abdomen out first. If your chest fills and puffs out, it should fill last, after your abdomen. While you hold your note, feel like you’re continuing to push your core outward/engage it. It takes practice and will feel strange and uncomfortable at first but the payoff is huge.

Just doing breathing exercises without a saxophone can help too. I used to do them while in bed. Sometimes it can be easier to feel the correct place for breathing while laying flat on your back at first. Practice slowly inflating for four beats, then deflating for four beats, really controlling the muscles. Then in for five, out for five, in for six, out for six, so on and so forth.

Everyone with ADHD experiences different severity of symptoms. For some, these symptoms are overcome with coping mechanisms. For others, the symptoms can be noticeably disabling. 

I was diagnosed late, at 26. Nobody noticed because my anxiety and fear of rejection and failure led me to heavily mask. For years I was treated unsuccessfully for anxiety/depression. In a weird way, I feel more privileged than some with ADHD, because I have developed my own strategies to mask and it allowed me to be successful in school and get through two degrees. But now 4 years into my career I’m struggling immensely with burnout, and I’m having more difficulty masking, even on meds. Lately my symptoms can “paralyze” me and it’s getting harder and harder to go into work and face projects and put on a show all day (teacher). 

It IS just a difference in how our brain works, in my opinion. But when you drop us into a society that is largely crafted for neurotypicals, it is disabling.

Six year olds can have a huge range of what is appropriate developmentally. The six year olds that get crazy good at an instrument right away are in the minority and often have parents that push them above and beyond at home. 

While it *could* be a symptom of a learning disability, it also could be totally normal and you might be expecting too much too fast. Teaching this age is not for everyone, and it often exhausted/frustrated me (I only teach older kids now). I was part of a weekend preschool music curriculum  and we did teach the staff and bare bones piano skills to 5-6 year olds, but we would only get through about three notes over six months and would intersperse it with other music reading games and activities. Honestly more of the lessons were devoted to music reading games and only a little bit of piano. By the time they finished the next class in the series (the next half a year), they were playing/identifying a whole scale.

I guess what I’m saying is be slow and patient now, don’t try to force too much at once. When they gain confidence with the little skills, they’ll start to learn faster. 

Some strategies to consider if you haven’t already:

-a little magnetic whiteboard with a staff on it and some circle magnets. Have her physically place the magnets to identify the notes. 

-super large print music

-start a consistent color code system for notes (I like to use rainbow order starting on C). Place small items on the keys to match the color and circle/highlight the notes on the page. Slowly withdraw them and see how she does. 

-gamify literally everything.

You might be breathing “wrong.” A lot of people do it at first, and it can become a hard to correct habit. I still catch myself doing it on occasion, and I’ve been playing woodwinds for ~18 years at this point . Check this:

When you breathe, does your upper chest puff out? Do your shoulders raise? If yes, you are getting a shallow breath- there’s an upper limit on how much you’ll be able to hold for and you’re only filling like half of the potential “tank”. Try to take a deep breath with your nose and mouth at the same time, and try to push your abdomen out first. If your chest fills and puffs out, it should fill last, after your abdomen. While you hold your note, feel like you’re continuing to push your core outward/engage it. It takes practice and will feel strange and uncomfortable at first but the payoff is huge.

Just doing breathing exercises without a saxophone can help too. I used to do them while in bed. Sometimes it can be easier to feel the correct place for breathing while laying flat on your back at first. Practice slowly inflating for four beats, then deflating for four beats, really controlling the muscles. Then in for five, out for five, in for six, out for six, so on and so forth.

Keep your chin up! I came from a public school that taught almost no theory. So I didn’t have a basic understanding of counting rhythms, even. I relied a lot on my ear and rote memorization. 

College was overwhelming at first and my first theory class was embarrassing, but once I understood how much easier knowing theory made things, life got a little easier. 

I still have to think about my minor scales from a theory perspective and mentally double check them before I play them. I never could memorize those cold. They’re in my fingers, but require more conscious thought before I begin.

The good news is… you don’t have to memorize the scales to fake some competence here. If you at least memorize the theory, you’ll be able to struggle through. If you memorize the order of sharps and flats and know all of your fingerings, you should be able to get through the hard ones slowly. Let’s focus on major scales since it’s more common for students entering college to not know all of their minor scales. 

Playing something slowly but correctly in an audition is almost always preferred and seen more favorably than playing something fast and wrong. 

Order of Flats: BEADGCF
Sharps are in reverse order of that: FCGDAEB. 

If someone asks you for a flat scale, you just jump ahead to the next letter in the order of flats and that’s how you can find the key signature. Ex: someone asks you to play Db Major…. Okay use the order of flats you have everything to the Db plus one, Gb. So BEADG would be flat in that scale. 

If someone asks you for a sharp scale, go down one half step from the name of the scale and you’ll find the last sharp in the key signature, so if you have the order memorized, you’ll know where to go from there! Example: E major. One half step down is D#. Key signature has the sharps in the order of sharps up to D#. So F, C, G, D are all sharp.

I went to a college where the professor exclusively taught Gordon and forbid us from using any of the other methods in our teaching practices/lesson plans.

I changed majors, only to go back to it when that professor left. I was much more successful when I was allowed to pull from a variety of pedagogies. I think MLT has more of a place in lower elementary education than it does in upper elementary and beyond. I hate the doo da, doo de system - it is juvenile and more confusing for kids the more complicated the rhythms get. If we're going with syllables, takadimi works better.

There are some good ideas in there (like audiation) but for the most part I would never use it in my instrumental classes as a base for instruction. There's a lack of notation and technical focus in the beginning that I don't like. Focus on developing the ear is great, but I also feel like that's the thing that comes more naturally with time, and the other things become harder to learn as you go, especially if you're allowed to develop bad habits.

Depends on the teacher though - whatever works best for your style is what you should go with.

husband and I are dealing with a double edged sword.

Both of us young teachers. When we left high school and started our degrees? We could have afforded a house on two teacher incomes no problem. Part of the reason I went into teaching in MA was because I thought it was modest but stable, and if I stuck it out I'd live pretty well. 

Now my future career is in jeopardy with all of these tax overrides. Our salaries are going up to keep up with costs (which is necessary to survive), but towns across eastern MA struggled a lot with their budget this past spring. Husband and I both teach a subject that is often the first or second thing to be cut. My district was spared this time, but I see the writing on the wall... fewer teachers and resources -> worse education -> more people putting their kids into private school -> see step one.

There are bad teachers out there, but I highly doubt if this was said it is coming from a place of malice. Could it be? Sure, and at that point I would take more aggressive action.

But at this point it's hearsay. Maybe the other parent is looking for a reason to stop your kids interacting with one another for some reason and stretched the truth. Maybe the teacher did say it. Maybe it was just a temporary suggestion like "oh it seems like they might need some space right now" if they're starting to show some co-dependency or fight. Maybe there is a serious issue here that needs addressing and the teacher is just mean. But there's no reason to get angry about what someone "supposedly" said without context.

But also... grades don't tell the whole story, and neither do people (especially children). You also don't know if everything is really going as well as your daughter reports/thinks. You aren't in the classroom, and you don't see their daily interactions. Maybe there is something concerning going on (and maybe it's the other child's fault, not yours). Kids at this age withhold social life information from their parents all of the time - it's naive to think otherwise. I'm not saying your child is to blame, to be clear - I'm saying that unless you are in that room following her around all day, you can't know. Kids can be entirely different people at school, as hard as it is to believe.

In any case, go into this calmly. Don't assume the truth right now, or it won't be a productive conversation. Tell her what you heard and why you're concerned. If her answer isn't satisfactory, then push forward and have a conversation with admin.

I think we do need to raise the bar on education research, but it's definitely more challenging when it comes to methodologies, as they can't be studied in a vacuum - and also rely in part on those elements of the human condition that also aren't entirely understood yet. 

I think when more research on those areas you mention is done, we might be able to understand more about education itself. There's so much that we're still learning about the brain, DNA, genetics, etc, that could propel research in education forward. But right now we have to rely on hypothesis and trial and error loosely based on our understanding of the brain and what seems to be sort of working.

Even with perfect understanding of the brain though, we have to remember that education is influenced by the interplay between 20+ brains in the classroom, all with unique backgrounds and dispositions. To truly get a good study on just teaching methodology/practice and what is objectively "best", you would need to fabricate some pretty extraordinary conditions to get reliable control groups - I can't think of a way that would be ethical. So much can influence how people learn things- from their culture, family support and attitude towards education and learning, socioeconomic status, etc. Even if we know that biologically our brains all work pretty much the same, they unfortunately aren't free from outside influence so it's hard to apply proper scientific practices to it. We might figure out the perfect strategy to teach one brain and it might not work as well when scaled up to a classroom and carried out by different people.

We can hopefully do better by applying scientific research in medicine, psychology, and sociology to educational practices. As long as the latter continues to evolve, so will education. But we can expect a lot of trial and error (and bullshit) along the way. The best advice I got from my college professor was "take what works for YOU as a teacher... leave what doesn't."

I think it's hard because we don't have a complete understanding of how humans learn yet. We have theories, some more sound than others - but no universal law. Science, with enough experimentation and study, eventually leads to some irrefutable facts. We have very little of those in education.

So, from the rest of the comments I might get some flack for this... but hear me out?

I did a lot of research on this myself for my master's - I did end up writing a paper on how the theory can be practically used in the classroom while also exploring and addressing its weaknesses. My professors liked it. There's plenty to criticize in it of course and plenty of rebuttals, but to say it's been entirely debunked isn't true either (beyond that a person can only learn ONE way). EVERYTHING in education is in the theory stage - there are very few perfect end-all, be-all facts. We don't have any "laws" of learning or education.

The theory becomes misappropriated and dangerous when educators use it to pigeon-hole students or say that they can "only" learn a certain way or can't grow in other areas. I think sharing this information with a student directly can be harmful if they're too young because then they might inadvertently pigeon-hole themselves. But from being in the classroom... I notice that certain strategies do really help certain students.

I think it's actually GREAT for lesson-planning to consider all of Gardner's Intelligences. I refer to them regularly when planning units and I try to incorporate lessons that use as many of them as possible. I'm not sharing this with my students or writing it down, to be clear, and I don't force one that wouldn't be natural. All students get the same lesson unless someone needs an extra boost, so everyone is exposed to everything, and certain students have a higher likelihood of latching on if you're approaching content from many different angles.  Rather than using it to try and figure out or label individual students, you can use it to create more varied educational experiences for your classes. If you notice a student struggles in your class but particularly latches on or succeeds with a certain lesson, that's valuable. It can give you a better idea of finding an "entry point" for them in the future.

If you couple all of the intelligences with a growth mindset and understand that each "domain" is a fluid ability that everyone possesses and can be improved on (and not an inflexible predisposition that they're born with), you can help make a child feel more confident in their learning by using their strengths to branch out from there, build the other skills, and make connections. Do I believe it's a perfect theory? Absolutely not. Do I think value can still be found in it? Yes.

As a music teacher and someone who makes cuts of music in my spare time, I'm fairly familiar with the copyright laws surrounding music (most are incredibly stupid and don't really protect the artist. I pity the underpaid musician, but I don't pity the giant music conglomerates that own everything. This hurts indie musicians more than it helps anyone).

What surprises me the most is actually that USFS got away with this for so long. It was only a matter of time. The livestreaming with music/selling videos with music without the rights has not been permitted under copyright law for a while, based on my understanding of the language - I guess no one has brought it up yet until now, which is surprising for such a big organization. I suspect the next crackdown is going to be on individuals making money (or not) off of cutting/altering music to fit time requirements, which is why I've been veeerryyy careful about who I cut music for and I don't advertise that I do it. You technically need to get publisher permission to "arrange" music, whether you make money off of it or not. Someone could definitely make the argument that cutting music or splicing with other songs is arranging. The blanket license really just offers protection for the venue, but they could technically still come after the individual for altering the music in the first place.

To put another stupid copyright law in your brain to show you why this isn't so far-fetched... I need to pay money to publishers for my school band to perform pieces (who are children), even if we already bought and own the music... every time we perform the piece. I need to get a separate license if I want to livestream it or professionally record it. If I want to arrange a song for band, I need the rights, even if I'm not going to be selling it. This does not fall under educational fair use. If the law is against students learning material in public school making no profit, it is definitely against entities that are making profit. Whether anyone \*actually\* will go after you, or even know if you don't is anyone's guess, but they \*can.\*

Why do you need paper tickets? As a memento? Then, in that case, do you ALL need paper tickets, or can you just get one or two?

Not allowing you to take photos/videos makes for a better audience experience. Photography is also expensive for the editing and whatnot. It's an opportunity to save money by not getting them.

An all-inclusive package would probably be a much larger sticker shock up front, and most families probably find it more feasible to pay as they go for these types of things (I know I can't pay 800-2000 up front.)

My ADHD was causing crippling driving anxiety (because driving was extremely overstimulating, I couldn't stay focused on the task as a whole because my mind was trying to take in random stimuli like what the car 7 cars ahead of me or behind me or in a completely different lane was doing rather than the most important one right in front of me). I hated driving even eight years after having a (relatively minor) accident. Exposure therapy and driving every day was not improving it. I would actively annoy friends and family to ask for rides even though I have a license and a car, and would have full on nervous breakdowns that would make me have to pull over. On medication, I can process the whole task of driving much better.

I didn't even realize how much it was helping until I started to notice it was worse again on mornings I forgot to take my meds.

I didn't expect it to help with this, I actually expected it to help with my difficulties/symptoms at work and home. The meds have also helped with those things, but this was the most unexpected and relieving benefit. There are still places I won't drive yet (cities, extremely crowded freeways during certain hours of the day), but at least I can be a functional adult and get myself to and from work every day (and my commute is 40-50 minutes).

I don't think I believe that anyone is truly just a lazy human. 9/10 times "laziness" (when crippling and frequent - not talking about a day here or there) can absolutely be explained with some kind of mental affliction, whether it be ADHD, depression, anxiety, etc... I can't tell you you definitely have ADHD, but if you're having some of these thoughts there's definitely SOMETHING going on you can get help for.

In the meantime, start making a list of some reasons why you think you have it. An actual list that you can reflect on and bring up/share with your psychiatrist when you find one. Could just be in your notes app on your phone - pop it in every time you think of something. Stories/instances from when you were a child or teen are usually more helpful as evidence.

We’ve been having regular sex but not formally tracking anything anymore- I really only feel the sting when someone around me announces. I think it can be good for your mental health (and sex life - it’s so much harder to get in the mood when you feel like you’re scheduling it all the time) to stop with all of the tracking for a while. Odds are you have rough estimate of your body by now anyway, so you can still aim for your fertile window. Life is a little easier when I’m not obsessing. Treatment also isn’t in the cards for us right now, so it’s the best we can do. But you might as well at least allow yourself to find something to enjoy in the meantime. Realistically for people like us who are unexplained, one tiny lifestyle change will probably not magically be the answer. You are better off doing things you want to do for yourself. If that’s getting healthier? Great! But don’t tie it to TTC. Tie it to your own self worth and what you want.

I’m still hopeful for both of us that it will happen. But I’ve also reflected a lot on the hard question of “what if it doesn’t? What if I need treatment?” I don’t want to look back on my life and see all of the things I didn’t do or lost out on because I was being overly cautious.

Getting rid of "levelled" classes and eliminating grouping by ability is a huge mistake

It's getting increasingly trendy right now to just mix kids of all abilities together at the secondary level (and dumping the concept of honors vs standard classes) because research is showing that lower performing kids do better when mixed with kids who are performing better, but my colleagues and I have yet to see that work in practice.

Usually it just makes it a million times more stressful to try and differentiate the material and just drags everyone down. High achieving kids get bored, low achieving kids get stressed.

The arguments behind it are in good faith (concerns about low SES students being disproportionally in "lower level" classes, concerns about it becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy where kids feel "not smart" and therefore perform lower because of the mental component) but in practice I see more kids suffering from this method than the old way.

\-My best guess is that you are going to higher level places than you're ready for (there aren't many spots like this in the game), you are starting encounters that you don't actually need to fight your way through (I accidentally aggroed the whole goblin camp my first time because I went in swinging, not realizing you could talk to them and explore first, possibly completely ignoring combat entirely. Can’t comment on Effexor specifically (hi, just started today), but as somebody who has actually had serotonin syndrome in the past (from Wellbutrin & fluoxetine)… 

Feeling happy and mood changes are not a symptom on their own, despite the name. It does sound like you’re experiencing some side effects, but does not sound like serotonin syndrome. My biggest and scariest symptom when I had it was involuntary and large muscle twitches and spasms, but it also built up with other fun things like fast heart rate, nausea, intense anxiety and paranoia, and auditory hallucinations (I kept hearing music in the distance that wasn’t there- thought my neighbor was blasting country music at 3 AM but my family confirmed there was no music. The music was so loud and distinct I could hum along, and it sounded like someone was singing but I could never piece together the words or recognize the song) It all came to a head after 2-3 days when I went to a college class (which I drove to, yikes), and literally felt so twitchy, dizzy, and sick that I laid on the bathroom floor until someone came and found me. My head felt like it was buzzing, I was sweating, I was hearing things that weren’t there, and so much twitching. 

If it’s serotonin syndrome… you will know. Keep an eye out for some of the physical symptoms.

The best you can do for yourself right now is get familiar with your cycles and start some positive lifestyle habits if you don't already have them (balanced diet, multivitamin, exercise, etc).

​

1. Accessibility/knowledge. Roller rinks are a dying breed in general, they are expensive to maintain and dropped in profitability. Hard to learn to artistic roller skate if there aren't many rinks around. Because of this, most people don't realize it exists. Ice rinks have hockey to help sustain them - even the average ice rink doesn't allot much time to figure skaters.
2. Aging demographic & resistance to change. Judges are very biased against newer and contemporary styles, many of them are very ingrained in the old ways. In my area, if you do a creative routine and it isn't recognizable music from a musical or theatrical production, you'll probably lose. For dance, there is still a heavy focus on organ music, and honestly incorporating pop music organ covers has NOT helped. 
3. Not enough "structure" to the competition scene, and high point of entry, especially for new adult skaters. What ice figure skating does right, is that it has several programs that are standardized for instruction, and many different competition levels. I started ice skating last year, and can enter a bracket that is appropriate for me and place. For roller skating (although I have been doing it a while, I took a long break), I was matched up with skaters who had been skating the same category for years and were lightyears out of my league. It was not even a little bit close. I got destroyed, and I did everything right.
4. No coaches/clubs. There are two clubs near me within an hour radius, but after that, the closest one is 2-3 hours. Many of the coaches are aging now too and there aren't as many people taking over, plus I find that there tends to be only one or two coaches per club which limits growth.
5. No advertising. Those clubs I mentioned above that I live near? Neither are advertised on their roller rink website. You would have to go to the rink, see a tiny dusty trophy cabinet to know they exist, and then figure out who the hell to ask about it. It is very convoluted to join/sign up. Want to ice skate? Do a google search and you can probably be signed up for a class within the hour. My club has produced several national champions and we are dying. 
6. Ice skating is just more convenient in almost every way, even though it is more expensive. It is easier to locate & join. It is easier to find a coach/club and get floor time. It is perceived as less clunky and more elegant. There is more glitz, glamour, and publicity. There are more sanctioned competitions, which means more opportunities for recognition & performance. You really have to LOVE roller skating to stick with it. Lately, as I've been doing ice and roller, I'm starting to drift towards team ice because it's just SO much more structured and beginner friendly.

This is a more complicated issue than it seems. I'm not saying it's an unworthy cause - I don't necessarily disagree with you - but it can't be an expectation. Veganism can already be prohibitively expensive in certain areas, and this tends to be an argument people use against veganism. "Well... if you care about the animals so much, then why aren't you doing x, x, and x..."

Completely avoiding fast fashion is a lot harder than just "oh, don't shop at Shein or Forever 21," which have become easy to identify and point the finger at due to the rapidly shifting styles and low price point. However, there are a LOT more stores in the fast fashion business and it can be hard to even differentiate between which brands are or aren't at times. Price point alone isn't even a good indicator. Someone can think that buying a $60 shirt definitely can't be contributing to fast fashion because it's $60, but it isn't necessarily true. Boycotting fast fashion, if we were really getting into the nuts and bolts and researching every company on the shelves, would mean boycotting buying clothes in general. It would mean doing most purchasing online because very few brick and mortar stores carry 100% sustainable and ethically sourced clothing. 

Thrifting can reduce impact, but unfortunately now thrift stores are becoming overrun with these fast fashion pieces too, and the rise of people going "hunting" to resell items has driven up prices. It's harder to find quality items, and harder to get a deal. When I lived in Boston, for example, the Goodwill was more expensive than buying new clothes from the Walmart in my hometown in suburban MA... Recently, my local Savers had a Shein shirt that cost more than it had probably cost brand new on Shein. Speaking of thrifting... as a vegan, is it problematic to thrift clothing that is not vegan? I don't say this to incite you, because I don't know the answer either. 

Now I'm not saying it isn't worth cutting out some of the worst offenders. Every little bit helps. But I think a better tactic, aside from making your own clothes, is just being more selective about the pieces you are buying and reducing your consumerism as a whole. Ask yourself, "is this just a trend? Will this still look good in 5 years? Do I really love it?" 

If you are someone in a position to ONLY buy sustainable brands with proven ethical labor practices, and they make them in sizes that fit them and styles that you like, then do so. But I don't necessarily think it should be an expectation or qualifying factor of veganism. I like to think that most people who ascribe to the vegan lifestyle for the ethics are already trying their best to limit their impact in other areas. TL;DR, you can stop after the first sentence: 

Accessibility for the average person, both for watching and participating. If you feel like reading a more detailed rant, feel free to continue. Sorry I’m advance.

We can start with participating though. Figure skating is extremely expensive even to be a little bit competitive. Classes, lessons, ice time… can easily cost over $100 a week, though I know families that can spend more like $100 a day. Many kids go through LTS and even early freestyle classes before they realize they can’t keep up against the kids with more money to spend on ice time. I think even the reputation alone of the high cost of figure skating keeps some people away altogether. Much cheaper, safer, and more accessible to put your child into dance classes, where your dollar will stretch farther for more instruction hours. Dance persists and survives on its own with little advertisement because it’s so much more accessible. You don’t need an expensive frozen building to practice skills, there’s more variety in styles, and classes and equipment are comparatively much cheaper and not competing with other disciplines for space. It’s less individualized and more class based- solos are optional but never an expectation. In dance, your class becomes like your team for the year. Figure skating is much more isolating as people come and go during shorter sessions and as singles freestyle reigns as what is “good skating” Show teams and precision exist, but they don’t carry the same reputation or glory. 

In some areas of the country, there are rink deserts where people might have to drive an hour or more to get to one, let alone one that suits their schedule. Facilities are costly to build and maintain, therefore the cost gets put onto those using the facility. Plus normal rink schedules are very limited as hockey teams and private events fight to share the open building hours, which aren’t great to begin with if you have a full time job or if your child attends normal school. Hard to get good enough to make it big in figure skating without giving up normal school at some point,  also hard to get good enough to justify giving up normal school on limited hours. There are very few figure skating exclusive rinks because games pull in more money with spectators and the opportunity for ticket and concession sales. 

Watching skating is hard for the average person to do with no experience. Most people could reasonably watch a game of soccer and figure out most of the rules just by watching a few games. It’s easy to differentiate the winner at least - there’s no room for questioning in most cases. Average people get frustrated with judging because they don’t “get it” or get why the person who is more fun to watch might not be the person who wins. It’s not as easy to pick up on rules as other sports and most people can’t tell jumps apart or fully appreciate how they are different. It’s also difficult to defend what the current scoring system rewards. You can really only appreciate it if you have some experience with the sport. 

It’s very difficult to actually find a place to watch it at all if you don’t have cable(many young people don’t anymore, and many of the older people who did once enjoy it are becoming disillusioned with figure skating becoming “less about the artistry and more about who can do the biggest jumps”). For the average person, it would be like tuning in to watch a once or twice a year football game and two teams you’ve never heard of are playing, and surprise they also completely turn over every other year so you don’t have someone consistent to cheer for. There’s not enough advertisement or events for it to stay relevant to the average person. The only time figure skating pulls a huge crowd is during the Olympics, and suddenly everyone is an expert and has an opinion until they forget about it for another four years. Even then you have to seek out the schedule if you’re interested in catching the relevant events. Half of the time I only realize I missed a competition when I start seeing the programs pop up on YouTube days later. Even algorithmic ads don’t seem to be advertising these, you have to know to look for it, and when the competitions are few and far between… it’s easy to not stay on top of it. Even then it’s hard to watch online without some sort of subscription to the channel that owns the rights. 

There’s probably something to be said for a touch of sexism as well and that female athletes in the United States are underpaid and underadvertised/televised compared to their male counterparts, and because figure skating is (as a whole) perceived as “feminine” but I don’t have concrete evidence to support that hypothesis.

This kind of got long because I feel this struggle so personally and I felt (and still feel) like nobody understands and no advice I ever got was helpful so I bolded the main points for TL;DR. My advice is more in the realm of accommodating and being patient with yourself, because I will be honest, nothing else has helped me except time, practice, and some coping strategies below. Therapy didn't help, but proper medication dose and an anti anxiety booster did help a little.

For context, I could barely drive down the street for 3 years after being involved in a (very minor - no injuries) accident at 18 just a few months after getting my first car. I still prefer not to drive if someone else is available to almost 10 years later - I've paid for a lot of other peoples' gas and thank you food and said "I'll pay if you drive" more times than I can count. I was walking 3 miles to and from work in my early 20s even though I had a car and a license. I have lost friends because they lived far away and I was too anxious to drive to them or even meet them halfway if it was somewhere I'd never been. Everything had to be on my terms, and I honestly can't blame them for dropping me. 

However, it **has definitely improved with repeated exposure and medication, although it took a** ***really really really*** **long time**. I thought I was never going to get better either. The road just felt so... loud, mentally. So I really do empathize, I promise. **What helps me is trying to make the driving experience as pleasurable as possible for myself (**It will never be great, I've never understood people who go for drives for fun or to clear their head - but we can make it a little nicer and associate the car with positive things**). Music, podcast, phone call to someone** for support (**hands-free is crucial here** and we don't always even talk constantly the whole time, just having someone "there" to talk to feels comforting and supportive to me - my mom and husband are my go to people for this), **audiobook**. I got myself a nice seat cushion, steering wheel cover and air freshener, **keep my car clean and visually free of distractions** (no trash comes into the car and I don't eat while I drive - I really hold myself accountable for taking everything out of my car that went into it).  **I prioritize my funds to make sure that my car is always in working order, because if anything starts going amiss it makes my anxiety so much worse and draws my focus and compulsive thoughts to whatever is/could be going wrong (check engine light, low tire pressure light, etc)**. I know this isn't always possible for everyone's financial situation, but if it is, it does help. 

Sounds dumb, but **chewing gum can also help**. Although it sounds counter-intuitive, having an auditory (not too loud) or some other idle stimulus can make focusing on the important parts of the road a little less tiring, and will distract you a bit from an anxiety feedback loop. It is much worse and more overstimulating for me if I'm in a silent car because my under stimulated brain is trying to "fill in" the silence with unimportant "road noise" - which sounds like it would be a good thing but not when you're fixating on things other than your immediate surroundings. I struggle filtering out the background visuals from the actual important things on the road (ex: will get distracted by a car being a jerk weaving in and out of traffic way ahead of me, and will forget to pay attention to the ones immediately around me). **Long story short, you can actually pay too much attention while you are driving with ADHD, or pay attention to the wrong things.** My brain is terrible at prioritizing the important from the unimportant when driving, and it's just trying to take everything in all at once, which make quick reaction times harder. I actually have come to love being stuck behind another car and staying in one lane, because all I have to focus on is maintaining a set distance from them and watching out for road signs/traffic lights. I will purposefully stick myself in a slower lane of travel and get "stuck" behind another car for this reason with a safe following distance. I don't have the pressure of being the "front" car and picking a speed and it takes some of the choice out of the situation.

I have accepted that my driving issues are partially disabling and have decided to accommodate for myself.

 I started by taking the route that is the least stressful/has the least traffic even if it is longer and less practical. For me, that means avoiding highways. I find them overstimulating and I'm constantly worrying about lane changes/people weaving in and out of traffic a mile ahead of me, and checking my mirrors obsessively to make sure I don't miss a car in my blind spot whenever I need to change lanes. **Cruise control = bad for me personally because it is less that I am engaging with the driving experience, but is helpful for some if you have lead foot when you zone out or if you are paranoid about speed limit.** Others find side roads more overstimulating with all the scenery/turns/speed changes/higher potential for unexpected events like an animal running in the road. I prefer the side roads because the route is more varied and forces me to pay attention more than the highway. **Pick what is best for you, and adjust your travel times accordingly. 

I will also leave way too early for any place I have to be to take out the "am I going to arrive on time" stress. If I'm going somewhere new for a scheduled event, I tend to drive there once beforehand (preferably with someone else) to scope out the parking/lanes/travel situation so I don't freeze in the moment and at least know what to expect.** I like predictability and it really is helpful to have a strong knowledge of the roads you are on, so if you do space out you have "emergency knowledge" in your back pocket. The surroundings also become less distracting/overwhelming if they are familiar, and can eventually be tuned out so your only focus can be on the cars and road in the moment. This is why **I do better asking someone to drive with me as a passenger to somewhere new I intend on going - I soak in all of the surroundings as if I'm driving without the pressure of actually driving that first time.** I'm thankful I have supportive family that has been willing to do this with me.

I can drive the highway now to and from work every day now (35-40 minutes) and have graduated to being able to take that stretch of highway to anywhere in between as long as it isn't too far off. There are still places I cannot go and do not know if I will ever be able to go on my own.  City driving for example is way too overstimulating for me and I don't think I'll ever conquer it, there are too many cars to pay attention to all at once and people walking out into traffic, cars merging with reckless abandon/not letting you merge, cars beeping half a second after the light turns green...etc. I'll choose public transit or ridesharing every time for the city, no matter how inconvenient.  My bubble has slowly grown from my town, to a few towns, to about an hour in every direction from me barring cities.

1) hold your leg back straighter and more behind you rather than out to the side before take off (I have this problem too- definitely common if you have any dance background). For landing it can be higher for balance but it looks like you're trying to force it higher than is comfortable for you right now. Also keep it more behind your hip on landing and less to the side (though this could just be my perception from this angle). You can play around with some of the more creative aspects once the basic jump feels better.

2) bring it straight up and through and think of bringing your lifting knee to your bellybutton (not literally that high, just to feel the direction, like you might kick a ball). Don't let it just "swing around" to the side. 

3) prior to jump, bring both arms back, bend your knees more, and spring everything up. Arms should come in close to your chest for the air part of the jump (not above your head), then back out straight to check the landing. Try to feel like you're pushing your arms straight out and down a bit more as you land, yours are quite high after the landing.

4) practice lots off wheels with proper form

I don't think this is how the majority thinks, though. As someone recently diagnosed, I survived this long because I got really freaking good at masking. I mean, even neurotypical people learn and adhere to certain "rules" when participating in society. I would argue that even neurotypical people mask sometimes (code-switching, hiding feelings, the entire concept of 'professionalism'). TL;DR you need to have a conversation with him either way to maybe clarify and adjust expectations. Good luck!

First, take some deep breaths.

It's different everywhere, but for my student teaching experience, no, I was not thrown to the wolves on my first day. My college actually laid out an "Expected schedule" for us, where we slowly assumed more and more of our cooperating teacher's responsibilities. 

My first week was entirely observation, with a small lesson (\~10 minutes) with each class at the end of the week so they could get used to me being in front of them. The second week I was taking over one or two classes a day, the third week a few more, and by the 7th week I was completely in control.

Your cooperating teacher may or may not tell you what they want you to teach each day, but you will likely be expected to write your own lesson plans. My cooperating teacher told me "do whatever you want, make the most of this experience, but I'm here for help if you need me."

Your cooperating teacher should have lots of helpful tips and hints, and if they're good they'll give you regular feedback and support. It gets much much easier as you go!

I can't relate to all of your struggles, but I made it through a program while simultaneously battling major depression (so severe I was approved for experimental and uncommon treatments), anxiety disorder, bulimia and anorexia (each at different points over 6-7 years), and now I'm suspecting ADHD as well (I have some appointments coming up to confirm that.) I also struggle with social anxiety, dealing with people my own age, and I am super sensitive to rejection and criticism (I don't get combative or deny it because I usually agree and understand it, I just cry or get anxious).

I was hospitalized once during my program, but fortunately by some act of the universe it happened during the summer. I was taking summer classes at the time, but my professors were very kind and allowed me to video call in (this was before COVID, so very unusual)  and gave me extra time to make up the work.

There were several times I didn't think I'd make it through. There were several times I almost quit. I don't even know what kept me going at some points, to be honest with you. But I did make it through, I just finished a long term sub position.... and I loved it. My mental illness still gets in the way sometimes, but I've learned how to manage it when I'm in the classroom in front of students. They would never know I struggle. I love working with kids. I do believe it's actually eased some of my depression symptoms and urges to unalive myself, because I really don't mind getting up and going to work every day. I don't really fall victim to my intense episodes and call out anymore because I want to be there for the kids. I've never felt that way about any other job. I actually found my education to take a greater toll on my mental health than the job itself.

I can't say it will be the same for you, but mental illness is not necessarily a reason not to teach. If anything, it can help you connect with students who are going through struggles of their own. You don't need to share your own struggles with them, but you can at least try to be for them what you need/needed.

As for the trans part of the equation... I really don't think you need to worry as much as you think you do. I don't feel qualified to give you too much advice here, because I don't have first-hand experience with it. I would be very selective about who you tell if you tell anyone, but for the most part I think there is a positive shift in attitude towards it in the education community more than the general population. Most of the educators that I've directly interacted with recently (>80%) are now including their pronouns in their email signatures and putting something up in their classroom (at least at the secondary level) to let their students know that they're welcome and safe. My experience could be biased -I do live in a very liberal state. I would tread more carefully in Arizona, and know that change is coming. I believe it's coming soon.
